question: Which EU institutions must receive the European Data Protection Board's public annual report under the GDPR?
gold_answer: The European Data Protection Board must make its annual report public and transmit it to the European Parliament, the Council, and the Commission.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:71::The Board shall draw up an annual report regarding the protection of natural persons with regard to processing in the Union and, where relevant, in third countries and international organisations. The report shall be made public and be transmitted to the European Parliament, to the Council and to the Commission.

question: Under the GDPR, what requirement applies when an EU country sets domestic rules governing how citizen ID numbers may be handled?
gold_answer: Where a Member State establishes specific conditions for processing a national identification number or other general-application identifier, it may be used only under appropriate safeguards for the data subject's rights and freedoms under the GDPR.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:87::Member States may further determine the specific conditions for the processing of a national identification number or any other identifier of general application. In that case the national identification number or any other identifier of general application shall be used only under appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of the data subject pursuant to this Regulation.

question: Does the GDPR add extra duties for telecom providers operating over public networks in the EU on issues already governed by parallel ePrivacy directive rules?
gold_answer: No; the GDPR does not impose additional obligations on processing connected to publicly available electronic communications services in public communication networks in the Union for matters where providers are already subject to specific obligations with the same objective under Directive 2002/58/EC.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:95::This Regulation shall not impose additional obligations on natural or legal persons in relation to processing in connection with the provision of publicly available electronic communications services in public communication networks in the Union in relation to matters for which they are subject to specific obligations with the same objective set out in Directive 2002/58/EC.

question: When may individuals give consent to broad areas of scientific research under the GDPR if full purposes cannot be identified upfront?
gold_answer: When it is not possible to fully identify the purpose of scientific research processing at data collection, data subjects should be allowed to give consent to certain areas of scientific research in keeping with recognised ethical standards for scientific research.
gold_evidence: gdpr:rec:33::It is often not possible to fully identify the purpose of personal data processing for scientific research purposes at the time of data collection. Therefore, data subjects should be allowed to give their consent to certain areas of scientific research when in keeping with recognised ethical standards for scientific research.

question: What kind of output must emerge from statistical analysis under the GDPR, and what restriction governs using it on named individuals?
gold_answer: Processing for statistical purposes implies that the resulting output is aggregate data rather than personal data, and neither that result nor the underlying personal data may be used to support measures or decisions regarding any particular natural person.
gold_evidence: gdpr:rec:162::The statistical purpose implies that the result of processing for statistical purposes is not personal data, but aggregate data, and that this result or the personal data are not used in support of measures or decisions regarding any particular natural person.

question: Under the GDPR, how may the Commission define electronic information-exchange arrangements between national regulators and the Board, and which external EU statute governs the required examination procedure?
gold_answer: The Commission may adopt implementing acts of general scope to specify arrangements for exchanging information electronically between supervisory authorities and with the Board, and those acts must be adopted using the examination procedure governed by Article 5 of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:67::The Commission may adopt implementing acts of general scope in order to specify the arrangements for the exchange of information by electronic means between supervisory authorities, and between supervisory authorities and the Board, in particular the standardised format referred to in Article 64. || gdpr:art:67::Those implementing acts shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 93(2). || gdpr:art:93::2. Where reference is made to this paragraph, Article 5 of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 shall apply.

question: When Brussels asks the EU privacy board for urgent input under the GDPR, can it set a turnaround deadline, and may outside actors direct the board's work?
gold_answer: When requesting advice from the Board, the Commission may indicate a time limit taking urgency into account; however, without prejudice to Commission requests, the Board must neither seek nor take instructions from anybody when performing its tasks or exercising its powers.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:70::Where the Commission requests advice from the Board, it may indicate a time limit, taking into account the urgency of the matter. || gdpr:art:69::Without prejudice to requests by the Commission referred to in point (b) of Article 70(1) and in Article 70(2), the Board shall, in the performance of its tasks or the exercise of its powers, neither seek nor take instructions from anybody.

question: Which authority signs off on multinational intragroup transfer frameworks under the GDPR, and which actors generally collaborate across the EU under the consistency mechanism governing that sign-off?
gold_answer: The competent supervisory authority approves binding corporate rules in accordance with the consistency mechanism; under that mechanism generally, supervisory authorities cooperate with each other and, where relevant, with the Commission to promote consistent GDPR application across the Union.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:47::The competent supervisory authority shall approve binding corporate rules in accordance with the consistency mechanism set out in Article 63 || gdpr:art:63::In order to contribute to the consistent application of this Regulation throughout the Union, the supervisory authorities shall cooperate with each other and, where relevant, with the Commission, through the consistency mechanism as set out in this Section.

question: On what condition may churches and religious associations keep applying their existing privacy frameworks under the GDPR, and how does the statute treat their national constitutional status?
gold_answer: Churches and religious associations or communities may continue applying comprehensive data protection rules that were already applied in a Member State at the time of the GDPR's entry into force, provided they are brought into line with the GDPR; the regulation respects and does not prejudice their existing Member State constitutional status as recognised in Article 17 TFEU.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:91::Where in a Member State, churches and religious associations or communities apply, at the time of entry into force of this Regulation, comprehensive rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to processing, such rules may continue to apply, provided that they are brought into line with this Regulation. || gdpr:rec:165::This Regulation respects and does not prejudice the status under existing constitutional law of churches and religious associations or communities in the Member States, as recognised in Article 17 TFEU.

question: Must a supervisory authority always perform its GDPR tasks free of charge for individuals and, where applicable, privacy officers, or when may it levy a fee or decline a request?
gold_answer: Each supervisory authority must generally perform its tasks free of charge for the data subject and, where applicable, the data protection officer; however, where requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, particularly because of repetition, it may charge a reasonable administrative-cost fee or refuse to act, bearing the burden of proving that character.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:57::The performance of the tasks of each supervisory authority shall be free of charge for the data subject and, where applicable, for the data protection officer. || gdpr:art:57::Where requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive, in particular because of their repetitive character, the supervisory authority may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs, or refuse to act on the request. The supervisory authority shall bear the burden of demonstrating the manifestly unfounded or excessive character of the request.

question: When the GDPR's statutory public-directory derogation applies to sending records to a third country or international organisation, what limits prevent exporting the whole database or sharing legitimate-interest entries with anyone?
gold_answer: Even when statutory consultation conditions for a public or legitimate-interest register are fulfilled, the transfer must not involve the entirety of the personal data or entire categories of personal data in the register, and transfers from a legitimate-interest register may be made only at those persons' request or if they are the recipients.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:49::(g) the transfer is made from a register which according to Union or Member State law is intended to provide information to the public and which is open to consultation either by the public in general or by any person who can demonstrate a legitimate interest, but only to the extent that the conditions laid down by Union or Member State law for consultation are fulfilled in the particular case. || gdpr:art:49::A transfer pursuant to point (g) of the first subparagraph of paragraph 1 shall not involve the entirety of the personal data or entire categories of the personal data contained in the register. Where the register is intended for consultation by persons having a legitimate interest, the transfer shall be made only at the request of those persons or if they are to be the recipients.

question: Under the GDPR's default-privacy obligation, how narrowly must a platform limit default processing, and may it expose records to an unlimited audience without the individual's action?
gold_answer: By default, a controller must implement technical and organisational measures ensuring that only personal data necessary for each specific processing purpose are processed; in particular, those measures must ensure that personal data are not made accessible by default to an indefinite number of natural persons without the individual's intervention.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:25::The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. || gdpr:art:25::In particular, such measures shall ensure that by default personal data are not made accessible without the individual's intervention to an indefinite number of natural persons.

question: Under the GDPR, how does sharing client or staff files across corporate affiliates for internal administrative purposes interact with rules governing transfers to non-EU group entities?
gold_answer: Controllers within a group of undertakings or affiliated to a central body may have a legitimate interest in transmitting client or employee personal data within the group for internal administrative purposes, without displacing the general GDPR principles for transferring personal data to a group undertaking in a third country.
gold_evidence: gdpr:rec:48::Controllers that are part of a group of undertakings or institutions affiliated to a central body may have a legitimate interest in transmitting personal data within the group of undertakings for internal administrative purposes, including the processing of clients' or employees' personal data. || gdpr:rec:48::The general principles for the transfer of personal data, within a group of undertakings, to an undertaking located in a third country remain unaffected.

question: For delegated measures adopted under the GDPR, how long is the objection window after notification, by how much may EU lawmakers extend it, and when can a measure take effect sooner?
gold_answer: A GDPR delegated act enters into force if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within three months of notification—a period extendable by three months at either institution's initiative—or earlier if both institutions inform the Commission before expiry that they will not object.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:92::A delegated act adopted pursuant to Article 12(8) and Article 43(8) shall enter into force only if no objection has been expressed by either the European Parliament or the Council within a period of three months of notification of that act to the European Parliament and the Council or if, before the expiry of that period, the European Parliament and the Council have both informed the Commission that they will not object. || gdpr:art:92::That period shall be extended by three months at the initiative of the European Parliament or of the Council.

question: How many days after its Official Journal release does the GDPR formally come into legal existence, and on what calendar date does it begin applying?
gold_answer: The GDPR enters into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union and applies from 25 May 2018.
gold_evidence: gdpr:art:99::1. This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. || gdpr:art:99::2. It shall apply from 25 May 2018.

question: On what calendar date did the EU's institutional privacy watchdog issue its formal consultation feedback during the drafting of the GDPR?
gold_answer: The European Data Protection Supervisor delivered its consultation opinion on 7 March 2012.
gold_evidence: gdpr:rec:172::The European Data Protection Supervisor was consulted in accordance with Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 and delivered an opinion on 7 March 2012 (17).

question: Does the GDPR grant Amazon Web Services an exemption from cross-border data transfer safeguards for its European cloud regions?
gold_answer: Not specified in the GDPR, which sets general rules and safeguard mechanisms for transfers to third countries and international organisations without naming Amazon Web Services or granting any vendor-specific cloud exemption.

question: Does the GDPR set a mandatory time interval or calendar schedule for testing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures?
gold_answer: Not specified in the GDPR; while controllers and processors must maintain a process for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures as appropriate, the regulation sets no numeric frequency, fixed interval, or calendar schedule.
